description:
Shrapnel | Planet X & SPHEREx
Building an interactive platform to explore SPHEREx observations and track changes across the sky. Looking for curious minds in astronomy, AI/ML, data science, and web development to turn space data into discoveries. Let's build something meaningful together!
Contact: arshbansal718@gmail.com
summary: BLINKSCOPE is a free web tool that turns NASA's SPHEREx all-sky infrared survey into a flipbook for any spot on the sky. Type an object name or RA/Dec and BLINKSCOPE finds every SPHEREx exposure covering that position, reads only the small patch needed straight from NASA's public SPHEREx archive, lines the patches up and plays them one frame per six-month sky pass, the same blink technique that found Pluto. Moving brown dwarfs, nearby stars and asteroids jump between frames, and variable stars brighten and fade. Users can stack SPHEREx's six detectors for cleaner images, subtract passes to highlight motion, view false-colour infrared, and click any source to build its 0.75–5 µm spectrum and light curve on the fly. With so much new SPHEREx data, discoveries need many eyes, and BLINKSCOPE gives anyone with a browser a way to look.
details:
WHAT IT DOES
BLINKSCOPE turns NASA’s SPHEREx all-sky infrared survey into a flipbook for any spot on the sky. Type an object name or coordinates (RA/Dec) and it finds every SPHEREx exposure of that position, lines them up, and plays them one frame per six-month sky pass, opening with a 2010 WISE image for a 15-year baseline. Anything that moves jumps between frames (Barnard’s Star jumps 2.7 arcminutes). It is the same “blink” method that found Pluto in 1930.

Features: PASSES and DIFF modes (DIFF shows only what changed: red = now, blue = before); IR COLOUR; stacking of SPHEREx’s six detectors (D1–D6) for cleaner images; click any star for its 0.75–5 µm infrared spectrum and light curve, built live; Gaia DR3 stars moved to each frame’s date with fast movers flagged; per-pixel contamination flags; a 3D sky globe; a guided interactive tour; SIMPLE and PRO modes; GIF export; a FLAG button to report candidate movers; and shareable/embeddable links (e.g. ?target=wise0855&mode=diff).

HOW IT WORKS
SPHEREx images are 65 MB files. BLINKSCOPE reads only the small strip around the target (~0.5 MB) directly from NASA’s public AWS copy using partial-file requests, so a flipbook loads in about 3 seconds with nothing to install. The browser applies each image’s astrometry and redraws every exposure on one fixed north-up grid, so real motion on the sky becomes visible motion. Per-pixel wavelengths come from SPHEREx’s spectral calibration, so each exposure contributes one point to the spectrum. New data releases are added by changing one line of configuration; the newest Quick Release (QR3) is already included.

TESTED AND VALIDATED
All five challenge targets work live: Barnard’s Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855−0714, RW Aurigae and R Draconis (plus bonus Luhman 16). WISE 0855, the coldest known brown dwarf, is detected at 10–14 times the noise level in every SPHEREx pass, exactly at its predicted moving position. The tool keeps working when NASA’s archive search is down (retries, caching and a saved listing for the challenge targets).

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT
Anyone, with no software or astronomy training, can inspect SPHEREx data for moving and variable objects within seconds, and share or embed what they find. Most known brown dwarfs and many comets were found by volunteers blinking images (e.g. Backyard Worlds); BLINKSCOPE brings that to SPHEREx so more eyes can make discoveries.

TOOLS
JavaScript (ES modules, no framework), HTML/CSS canvas, Node.js serverless functions on Vercel, Aladin Lite v3, NASA/IPAC IRSA services, NASA AWS Open Data, ESA Gaia archive, NASA MAST, CDS Sesame. 16 automated tests. Code: https://github.com/asherbnsl/spherex-sky-eye

CREATIVITY
A cinematic “mission control” interface inspired by God’s Eye View; a 15-year WISE-to-SPHEREx blink; spectra built on the fly from SPHEREx’s 102 colours; in-browser decoding of SPHEREx contamination flags; a smooth flight across a 3D sky globe to each target.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED
Speed on ordinary internet (partial reads, no big downloads); ease of use for the public (guided tour, simple mode); scientific honesty (contamination flags, labelled approximations); reliability when archives are busy; security (no logins or personal data, escaped inputs, strict security headers); easy updates for new data releases.

WHAT IS FUTURE WORK (NOT BUILT YET)
Automatic sky-wide mover search; asteroid and comet mode using orbits; a moderated public list of community flags; calibrated photometry for very bright, saturated stars.
